1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6.name: Ruy Lopez: Berlin Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6.background: Common in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when Emanuel Lasker played it, it declined afterwards. Vladimir Kramnik revived it in the 2000 World Championship match, using it four times to draw against Garry Kasparov.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.O-O.strategy: Castles and lets Black take on e4, since the pawn is regained by pressure on the e-file against the uncastled king. White gets the safest king and the simplest development, and the result is solid, often drawish play with little risk.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.O-O.name: Ruy Lopez: Berlin Defence

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.d3.strategy: Defends e4 solidly, so that ...Nxe4 is no longer a threat and the pressure on e5 is real: Bxc6 and Nxe5 threatens to win a pawn. White gives up the quick d4 for a slower, manoeuvring game.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.d3.name: Ruy Lopez: Berlin Defence, Anti-Berlin Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.d3.background: Wilhelm Steinitz scored many spectacular successes with 4.d3 during his reign as World Champion.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.d4.strategy: Strikes at e5 at once, but leaves e4 unprotected, so Black can take it or capture on d4. The result is open, level play, and White gets none of the extra safety that castling or d3 would give.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.Nxe5.strategy: Sacrifices a knight for a pawn, hoping to drive the recapturing knight away with d4 and e5. But Black's knight simply retreats to g6 and White has no compensation for the lost piece.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.Nxe5.name: Ruy Lopez: Halloween Attack

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.d3 Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop to its most active square, eyeing f2 and the d4 square. It also sets a tactical point: if White trades on c6 and grabs e5, the queen jumps to d4 with a fork and the threat of mate on f2. Black fights for the centre with pieces in a manoeuvring game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.d3 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn, the solid answer to the extra pressure 4.d3 puts on it. The cost is that the king's bishop has only e7 as a natural square, so Black settles for a slow, closed game in which White chooses the pace.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.d3 Ne7.strategy: Moves the same knight twice and blocks the king's bishop, so Black falls behind in development; the only point is a trap. If White grabs the pawn on e5, the reply ...c6 wins a piece. Met calmly, Black is simply a tempo down.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.d4 exd4.strategy: Captures the pawn rather than defending e5, which opens the e-file and leads to open play. Black is a pawn up for the moment, but the king is still in the centre, so Black must meet White's quick development accurately.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.O-O Nxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn at once. It is more an exchange than a gambit, because White wins it back easily on the half-open e-file while Black's king is still in the centre. Black accepts open play in return for the most solid, and often drawish, positions.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.O-O Bc5.strategy: Develops the bishop to its most active square, eyeing f2 and the castled king, while keeping the e4 pawn under attack. Black avoids the heavy theory of the main line and asks White to build the centre while watching f2.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.O-O d6.strategy: Reinforces e5 with a pawn and keeps the position compact. It is solid but passive: the king's bishop is limited to e7, and White gets the freer game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.O-O Ng4.strategy: Steps away from the centre to set a trap: after h3 and ...h5, taking the knight opens the h-file for a dangerous attack. When White does not bite, the knight is only driven back and Black has lost time.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 Nf6 4.O-O Ng4.name: Ruy Lopez: Berlin Defence, Fishing Pole Variation
